About this project

A source-led record of West Bengal OBC policy

This independent research archive brings together publicly available notifications, statutes, public-hearing notices, policy reports, and selected court records concerning Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in West Bengal, and publishes them online for free public access.

Purpose

Make the record easier to examine

The project is designed as a chronological research desk. It helps readers trace a claim from a timeline entry to a notification, a hearing notice, a policy source, or a court record without treating summaries as a substitute for the original document.

Scope

Policy, process, and litigation

The archive covers the statutory framework, State OBC-list changes, reservation and roster records, the 2025–26 notification sequence, public hearings, and a growing litigation tracker. It does not claim to be a complete government archive.

Use with care

Research aid, not legal advice

Some records are text-extracted or copied from publicly accessible mirrors. Court status, operative directions, and notification validity should always be confirmed from the issuing authority or the relevant court.

How records are handledWhat this means
Published onlineThe archive is hosted on the open web and served straight from the repository — no download or installation needed.
Source labelsEntries distinguish official downloads, scanned/text-extracted records, and mirror copies that need verification.
Large case bundlesVery large filings are catalogued but not added by default; this keeps the site fast and practical to maintain.
Corrections and additionsUse the Add Record guide's fields to record date, authority, status, source URL, and the affected notification or case.
Source principle: where this site summarizes a record, open the linked document and treat the primary source as controlling. The project does not endorse any political position or make findings about any community.

Who maintains this?

This archive is built and maintained by a small team of volunteers, supported by the Civic Research Group community. It is an ongoing effort: notifications, court records, and policy reports are added as they are collected and verified, and the coverage keeps growing. If you hold a document, a correction, or a gap we have missed, the Contribute page is the fastest way to help improve the record.

What OBC Means

OBC is a constitutional-administrative category for socially and educationally backward classes. It is not a religion quota, and it is not limited to Hindu caste names.

Core idea

OBC is about backward classes

“Other Backward Classes” refers to communities or classes identified as socially and educationally backward and inadequately represented. In practice, state lists use caste, sub-caste, occupation, community, conversion history, and social location as evidence markers, but the legal category is backward class.

Common myth

“Muslims have no caste, so they cannot be OBC”

That is too simple. Islam as a faith does not prescribe caste, but South Asian Muslim society has long had socially ranked occupational and descent communities. Groups such as Jolah/Ansari-Momin, Fakir/Sain, Nashya-Sekh, Pahadia Muslim, Rayeen/Kunjra, Hajjam, and Chowduli appear in West Bengal OBC records because the class or community was treated as backward, not because reservation was given to all Muslims.

How to read the files

Community evidence still matters

The useful question is not whether a whole religion has caste. The useful question is whether a particular class has evidence of social and educational backwardness, inadequate representation, and proper process through the Commission, survey, hearing, or notification route. This page keeps those source trails visible.

Scientific Methods for Determining Backwardness

A fair OBC decision should be evidence-led: define the class, measure social and educational disadvantage, test representation in public institutions, publish the data trail, and periodically review whether the benefit is reaching the intended class.

Step 1 · Define the unit

Backwardness is class-specific

The correct unit is not an entire religion or a vague surname group. It is the specific caste, sub-caste, occupational community, converted community, or locally known class whose disadvantage can be measured. West Bengal records show this logic: entries such as Bhangi (Muslim), Sekh/Seikh, Kazi/Kaji/Quazi/Quaji (Muslim), and SBCW-165 Category-B serial 97 are document-specific, not blanket religious reservation.

Step 2 · Measure disadvantage

Use multiple indicators, not one slogan

The Mandal framework grouped indicators into social, educational, and economic heads and used a weighted score. That is the right spirit: no single number proves backwardness by itself. A robust method checks school completion, literacy, dropout, landholding, occupation, housing, income, social stigma, manual or hereditary work, and exclusion from public posts.

Step 3 · Publish representation

Reservation depends on inadequate representation

Backwardness is incomplete without representation data. Departments should publish class-wise and category-wise counts in recruitment, promotions where relevant, educational admissions, scholarships, hostels, certificate issuance, and pending vacancies. Without this, the public cannot test whether a class is under-represented or whether benefits are being captured by better-placed groups.

Evidence question Data needed Good method Misuse risk
Is the class socially backward? Local social status, traditional occupation, endogamy, residential segregation, stigma, dependence on low-status work, field verification. Household survey plus public objections, local body verification, and Commission hearing notes. Relying only on political claims, pressure groups, or community labels without field evidence.
Is it educationally backward? Literacy, school completion, dropout, higher education participation, gender split, district-wise variation. Compare class data with state average, district average, SC/ST/OBC averages, and non-reserved groups. Using only poverty data or only one district while ignoring education gaps elsewhere.
Is it economically vulnerable? Landholding, income band, occupation, housing, credit access, asset ownership, informal work, migration. Use economic indicators as supporting evidence, then apply creamy-layer exclusion to avoid elite capture. Treating poverty alone as OBC backwardness; poverty policy and backward-class policy overlap but are not identical.
Is representation inadequate? Class/category-wise share in government jobs, educational admissions, public bodies, certificates, applications, selections, and vacancies. Publish department-wise annual data with sanctioned posts, filled posts, applicant pool, selected candidates, and backlog. Declaring under-representation without publishing denominators or without separating applicants from selections.
Did the process allow correction? Public notice, hearing date, objection register, evidence submitted, Commission advice, reasoned order. Link every notification to hearing notices, survey records, advice reports, and final reasons. Fast notification without a visible evidence trail, which later becomes vulnerable in court and public debate.

Why Caste Census and Departmental Data Matter

A caste or class census is not useful because identity labels are magic. It is useful because policy needs denominators. Representation data is the numerator. Together they let the public ask whether reservation is proportionate, under-inclusive, over-inclusive, or captured.

Population denominator

If a class has no reliable population estimate, every percentage argument becomes guesswork. The 2012 panchayat survey documents in this bundle show the practical problem: officials were instructed to enumerate households, carry the backward-class list, publish draft lists, and process claims and objections. That kind of procedure is the beginning of auditable data.

Open 2012 survey trail

Representation numerator

Departments should publish annual tables showing how many people from each OBC category and, where legally and administratively possible, each listed class are present in services and admissions. This is how one can distinguish genuine inadequate representation from a merely loud demand.

Outcome audit

Reservation should be checked against outcomes: who received certificates, who applied, who was selected, who remained excluded, which districts lagged, and whether the creamy layer is filtering better-off households. Good data protects deserving groups and exposes misuse.

Real example in this file What it teaches Data still needed
2010 Category-A / Category-B split Classification can separate "more backward" from "backward" classes, but the public needs the underlying scoring or reasons to evaluate placement. Class-wise scores, criteria sheet, Commission advice, and representation table used for A/B placement.
2012 panchayat backward-class survey instructions The PRD order trail is a strong real example: it required GP constituency-wise survey units, Census/SECC/electoral roll reference records, local enquiry, draft publication, claims and objections, final publication, and software-based compilation. Final constituency/GP/block/district population tables, filled Annexure-C/D/E compilations, objection disposal registers, and the published final household lists.
2025 public hearing notices Hearings show that process existed, but notice alone does not prove backwardness. Attendance, submissions, survey findings, Commission reasons, and the class-wise advice behind each recommendation.
2026 withdrawal of 2025 notifications A weak or disputed evidence trail can destabilize policy and create uncertainty for beneficiaries and administrators. Clear public explanation of which evidence failed, which records remain valid, and what fresh process will replace them.

Good Uses and Misuses of OBC Reservation

Good side

Correcting structural exclusion

When applied to classes with proven social and educational backwardness and inadequate representation, reservation opens access to jobs, education, hostels, scholarships, and public legitimacy. It can convert invisible occupational communities into recognized citizens with a measurable route into public institutions.

Good side

Forcing the state to measure society

A serious OBC process requires surveys, hearings, lists, objections, certificate rules, and roster data. That can improve governance beyond reservation itself because the state must publish who is excluded, where, and why.

Misuse

Elite capture and vote-bank listing

Misuse happens when powerful subgroups enter without evidence, when creamy-layer rules are weak, when politically useful communities are added quickly, or when no one publishes outcomes. This harms genuinely backward classes because the benefit pool is diluted and public trust falls.

What do we lack more? In this bundle, the largest gap is not the final notifications. It is the underlying data: class-wise population denominators, class-wise representation in departments and admissions, Commission advice reports, benchmark survey tables, hearing records, objection-disposal registers, and annual outcome audits. The next best improvement would be a public evidence matrix linking every listed class to population, education, occupation, representation, hearing, Commission advice, notification, and later review.

Policy Reports & Backwardness Criteria

These are not West Bengal notification files, but they explain the policy architecture used to understand OBC identification, Muslim OBCs, affirmative action, and evidence requirements.

1980 · Mandal Commission

Criteria for identifying socially and educationally backward classes

The Mandal Commission is the baseline framework for OBC policy. Its relevant section groups backwardness indicators under social, educational, and economic heads, uses a weighted score, and treats 11 points out of 22 as the threshold in its survey method. It also notes that caste-based indicators needed a separate approach for non-Hindu backward communities.

  • Use here: evaluate whether a notification or class-wise report explains social, educational, and economic backwardness.
  • Relevant chapters: socio-educational field survey, criteria of backwardness, identification of OBCs, recommendations.
Open PDF
2006 · Sachar Committee

Muslim OBCs and affirmative action

The Sachar report supplies the national evidence layer for Muslim social, economic, and educational conditions. Chapter 10 is especially relevant because it treats Muslim OBCs as a distinct analytical category and compares education, employment, poverty, landholding, and access to entitlements.

  • Use here: distinguish religious identity from backwardness evidence and locate Muslim OBC disadvantage in measurable indicators.
  • Relevant chapter: “The Muslim OBCs and Affirmative Action.”
Open PDF
2015 · West Bengal research

Muslim OBCs in West Bengal

This research note links Mandal, Sachar, and West Bengal lists. It discusses Muslim OBC population estimates, classification issues, implementation problems, and the state’s Category-A/Category-B framework.

  • Use here: contextualize West Bengal-specific Muslim OBC entries and gaps in identification or benefit delivery.
  • Relevant sections: Muslim OBC population, proforma/listing in West Bengal, implementation problems.
Open PDF
2011 · NCBC advice compilation

Central OBC advice concerning West Bengal

This 80-page compilation begins with National Commission for Backward Classes advice concerning West Bengal communities. It is included as a source collection for Central-list context; it does not itself determine the current State OBC list.

  • Use here: trace Central Commission advice and compare it carefully with State notifications.
  • Source care: archived scan; confirm the original NCBC record before relying on individual pages.
Open PDF
Commission survey proforma

Block-level evidence template

The West Bengal Commission for Backward Classes proforma asks for block-wise population, social background, education, occupation, representation, and comparative local information. It is a useful example of the evidence trail that should accompany a class-identification exercise.

Open PDF
2015 · National Commission for Backward Classes

Sub-categorisation within OBCs

This NCBC report was prepared for the Central List and considers methods, categories, and related issues for sub-categorisation. It is national policy context, not authority for the West Bengal State List or a substitute for a State notification.

  • Use here: compare proposed sub-categorisation methods with the evidence and process used in State exercises.
  • Source care: archived scan dated 2 March 2015; verify the primary NCBC publication before relying on specific recommendations.
Open PDF

Amal Chandra Das v. State of West Bengal

WPO 60 of 2011 WPA 22145 of 2010 WPO 1160 of 2013 WPO 578 of 2012

The 22 May 2024 judgment struck down the OBC classification of 77 classes made from 2010 and the OBC certificates issued on that basis, while protecting people already appointed. The State's appeals against it were withdrawn on 14 July 2026.

WPA 21501 of 2026 (Hasibur Rahaman Mondal) WPA 23207 of 2026 (Mehebuba Khatun) WPA 23209 of 2026 MAT 1374 of 2026 SLP(C) 31121 of 2026

NEET-UG 2026 candidates who sought to switch to EWS after results, and SLST 2025 candidates who sought OBC-A reserved status, both lost. The Court held that category must be valid on the application date and that the 2024 judgment was final before the SLST recruitment began. The Division Bench upheld the NEET-UG ruling on 18 August 2026, and the Supreme Court closed the challenge on 5 October 2026, saying the EWS benefit would be available next year.

Cases on how ongoing recruitments handle candidates whose OBC status fell away. SLST candidates may be considered as EWS after verification (review refused); candidates already selected as OBC-A are outside the 7 August 2026 notification; candidates dropped from the list may compete as EWS in police recruitment. Whether the new roster can apply midway through a selection is pending before the Chief Justice's Bench.

Litigation support note · not an official order

Legal principles for existing OBC-certificate appointees

A user-supplied bilingual note argues that bona fide employees appointed on government-issued and verified OBC certificates should not face blanket termination merely because a reservation policy or class-list process is later invalidated. Treat this as an argument map: verify every citation against the actual judgment before using it.

Factual premise

No fraud or false claim

The note’s protection argument depends on the employee having acted in good faith, without misrepresentation, and on certificates having been issued and verified by competent government authorities before appointment.

Service finality

Completed appointments

It distinguishes policy validity from appointment validity and says completed recruitment, seniority, promotion, pension, vested rights, and livelihood interests require individualised treatment.

Process safeguard

No blanket cancellation

The note relies on Articles 14, 16, and 21, natural justice, proportionality, legitimate expectation, and administrative fairness to oppose mass termination without hearing.

Ground from the noteShort argument preserved from the DOCXLegal hook cited in the note
No fraud or misrepresentationEmployees did not secure appointment by deception; the certificates were government-issued and were relied on in good faith.Article 14; doctrine of good faith; rule of law
Government verificationThe appointing authority verified the certificate before employment, so a later policy defect should not be equated with employee misconduct.Articles 14 and 16; service jurisprudence
State-caused administrative errorThe State should not punish innocent employees for its own administrative acts or lapses.Article 14; administrative fairness; doctrine of fairness
Policy validity versus appointment validityInvalidity of a policy or class-list process does not automatically invalidate all appointments already completed under government-issued certificates.Milind; Article 142
Long service and vested rightsLong service creates reliance interests in salary, seniority, promotion, retirement benefits, pension, and career stability.Doctrine of vested rights; right to livelihood under Article 21
Natural justiceNo employee should be removed by a blanket order without notice, individual hearing, and a specific finding.Audi alteram partem; Articles 14 and 21
Collective punishmentThe note rejects mass termination because constitutional liability should be individual, not collective.Articles 14 and 21; proportionality
Burden of proofFraud, false claim, or illegality should be proved by the person alleging it.Sections 101-102, Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Re-verification limitsBlanket re-verification or reopening of completed verification requires lawful authority and should not be arbitrary.Rule of law; Article 14; finality
Public interest and stabilityContinuity of service supports public administration and avoids disruption from large-scale dismissal.Public interest doctrine; Article 142
ThemeHow the note uses itCited authorities to verify
Bona fide appointment protectionInvalidation of caste status or policy should not automatically undo completed appointments where there is no fraud.State of Maharashtra v. Milind (2001) 1 SCC 4; Kavita Solunke v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 8 SCC 430
Fraud exceptionProtection is weaker or unavailable if appointment was obtained through fraud or a false caste claim.R. Vishwanatha Pillai v. State of Kerala (2004) 2 SCC 105; Chairman, FCI v. Jagdish Balaram Bahira (2017) 8 SCC 670
Non-arbitrariness and livelihoodMass dismissal after long service may be attacked as arbitrary, disproportionate, and harmful to livelihood.E.P. Royappa (1974) 4 SCC 3; Maneka Gandhi (1978) 1 SCC 248; Olga Tellis (1985) 3 SCC 545
Reliance on government actionEmployees may argue legitimate expectation, promissory estoppel, good faith, and administrative fairness because they relied on official certificates and verification.Navjyoti Co-operative Group Housing Society (1992) 4 SCC 477; Hindustan Development Corporation (1993) 3 SCC 499; Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills (1979) 2 SCC 409
Recruitment finalityThe note says completed recruitment should not ordinarily be reopened after many years, especially without individual findings.K. Manjusree v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2008) 3 SCC 512; State of Punjab v. Jagdip Singh, AIR 1964 SC 521
Constitutional / doctrinal labelUse in the note
Article 14Opposes arbitrary cancellation and demands fairness by the State.
Article 16Frames public employment as requiring non-arbitrary, equal treatment of already appointed employees.
Article 21Links long-standing government employment with livelihood and dignified continuity.
Article 142Supports a complete-justice argument for protecting bona fide employees where facts justify it.
Legitimate expectationEmployees relied on official certificates, official verification, and completed recruitment decisions.
Promissory estoppelThe note argues that the State should not resile from its own representation after citizens acted on it.
ProportionalityMass dismissal is presented as disproportionate where the alleged defect is administrative or procedural.
Finality and good faithCompleted recruitment should not be reopened after years unless fraud or a legally sufficient ground is shown.
Use discipline: this note is useful for framing questions in employee-protection litigation, but it is not a substitute for the operative order in the pending West Bengal OBC matters. It should be read with the fraud exception in Vishwanatha Pillai and Jagdish Balaram Bahira, and with actual court orders, pleadings, and verified SCC/official judgment links before treating any principle as controlling.

Framework for New & Missing Entries

Use this structure whenever a new PDF, court order, hearing notice, report, or missing source is added. The goal is to keep every entry searchable, source-linked, and auditable.

1. Minimum fields for every document

  • Date: ISO format, for example 2025-06-03.
  • Document number: notification/order/memo/case number exactly as printed.
  • Document type: notification, order, corrigendum, hearing notice, court order, report, act, roster, certificate guideline.
  • Status: current, withdrawn, superseded, legacy, missing, draft, or verification-needed.
  • Short summary: one sentence describing legal or documentary effect.
  • Source: published PDF URL plus source authority, when known.

2. Evidence checks before marking complete

  • Does the PDF text match the notification number, date, and printed title?
  • Does it add, amend, withdraw, classify, or merely implement another document?
  • What earlier document does it cite, and what later document changes it?
  • For inclusion/categorisation: is there a Commission advice, survey, hearing, or benchmark record?
  • For court records: what operative direction affects the current list or reservation percentage?

3. Missing-entry statuses

  • Not yet archived: known source exists, file not yet added.
  • Source not found: cited in another record, original PDF not located.
  • Partial: source found only as quote, mirror, OCR, or bundled page inside another PDF.
  • Needs OCR: scanned source exists but text is not searchable.
  • Verification needed: source exists but date/number/content conflict needs checking.

Completeness Audit

The archive contains the core 2010, 2025, and 2026 notifications and a substantial public-hearing notice set. The remaining procedural gap is the West Bengal Commission for Backward Classes record behind the notices: benchmark-survey memos, class-wise advice reports, survey data, and later court records around the 2025 survey challenge.

Found online from original sources

Official BCW order indexes, official WBCBC public-hearing notice list, and the official 2025 notification-wise OBC list.

Partly found

Benchmark-survey memos are quoted or mirrored online, but the original Commission PDF locations still need recovery or download from the department/Commission if available.

Not yet archived

Class-wise Commission advice/survey reports, the benchmark-survey memo trail, complete court filings/orders after the 2025 survey challenge, and original source pages for hearing notices currently represented only by archived scans.
